You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 2 of 12.

RESULTS OF YOUR PREVIOUS ROUND:

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor-node load RL from a piezo transducer.
    *   Requirements:
        *   `vout_min`: `vavg >= 1.8 V`
        *   `vout_max`: `vmax <= 3.6 V`
        *   `ripple`: `vpp <= 0.05 V`
        *   `startup`: `tup <= 0.4 s`
        *   `settled`: `dv <= 0.02 V`
    *   Piezo characteristics: Low voltage (3.2V open-circuit), high impedance.
    *   Operating Conditions: S1-S6 (variations in Ip, f, Cp, RL, Temp).

    *   `sshi_fbr`: Combined SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor) and FBR (Full Bridge Rectifier).
        *   The inductor/switch was placed in parallel with the piezo (`pzp` to `pzn` via `n1`).
        *   The FBR was in parallel with that.
        *   Result: Very poor. `vavg` failed for most cases. This is likely because the FBR diodes (even DSCH) have a voltage drop that is too high for the low open-circuit voltage (3.2V) of the piezo, and the SSHI circuit as connected might be interfering or not providing the intended voltage boost.
    *   `sece_sym`: Failed screen. Symmetry probably didn't help.
    *   `fbr_zener`: Failed screen. Standard FBR is inefficient here because of the diode drops relative to the source voltage (3.2V).

    *   Open-circuit voltage $V_{oc} = \frac{I_p}{2 \pi f C_p} \approx 3.2\text{ V}$.
    *   Standard bridge rectifier: $V_{out} \approx V_{oc} - 2 V_{forward}$. With $V_{forward} \approx 0.25\text{ V}$, we have $V_{out} \approx 2.7\text{ V}$ *ideally*, but the piezo is a current source. The voltage across the piezo capacitance $C_p$ must rise high enough to overcome the diode drops.
    *   SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor) is designed to flip the voltage on $C_p$ at the peaks, effectively increasing the voltage available to the rectifier.
    *   The `sshi_fbr` implementation had a problematic connectivity: the SSHI inductor path was in parallel with the FBR.
    *   A classic SSHI circuit typically uses a switch and an inductor to invert the voltage on $C_p$, followed by a half-wave or full-wave rectifier.

    *   *Topology A: SSHI with Half-Wave Rectifier (Standard).*
        Piezo (pzp, pzn). Switch and inductor for inversion. One diode to output.
        Wait, if the piezo voltage is low, a full-bridge might be too lossy. But a half-wave only harvests half the cycle.
    *   *Topology B: SSHI with Full-Bridge Rectifier (Corrected).*
        The inductor and switch should invert the voltage on the piezo capacitance.
        The rectifier should then take that voltage.
        Current flow: Piezo charges $C_p$. At the peak, the switch closes, $L$ flips the charge on $C_p$.
        The FBR is connected as usual.
    *   *Topology C: Synchronous Rectification (using switches).*
        The problem description says we have "at most 4 switches".
        A full synchronous rectifier would need 4 switches.
        `S1`: pzp to out, `S2`: pzn to out, `S3`: 0 to pzp, `S4`: 0 to pzn.
        Controller `G1` (both edges) could toggle these. But the `SYNC` controllers provided only have `ton` and `phase`. They aren't complementary.
        If we have two `SYNC` controllers:
        `G1` (pos peak): closes switch `S1` (pzp to out) and `S3` (0 to pzn)? No, that's not how `SYNC` works.
        `G1` closes `S1` for `ton`. `G2` closes `S2` for `ton`.

    *   Let's look at the SSHI logic:
        1. Piezo charges $C_p$ to $V_{peak}$.
        2. Switch $S$ closes for $t_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$, transferring energy from $C_p$ to $L$ and back to $C_p$ with opposite polarity.
        3. This increases the voltage swing.
        4. Rectifier converts this to DC.

    *   Let's refine the "SSHI + Half-Wave" or "SSHI + Full-Wave":
        If we use a full-bridge, we lose $2 \times 0.25 = 0.5\text{ V}$.
        If the $V_{oc}$ is 3.2V, the peak is 3.2V. SSHI can potentially double the effective voltage seen by the rectifier.

    *   Let's try a simpler approach first: **A standard SSHI with a half-bridge/diode.**
        Actually, for low voltage, we need a very efficient path.
        What if we use a synchronous rectifier for one half and a diode for the other? Or just a simple SSHI with a single diode?
        SSHI (L, S) + Diode (D1) + Capacitor (C1).
        Circuit:
        L1: pzp to n1
        S1: n1 to pzn (Ctrl G1: both edges)
        D1: pzp to out
        C1: out to 0
        Wait, if the switch is on "both" edges, it flips the piezo voltage $V_{pzp}-V_{pzn}$ every half cycle.
        This means $V_{pzp}$ will oscillate around 0 but with a higher amplitude.
        If D1 is from pzp to out, it harvests the positive peaks.

    *   Wait, the FBR in `sshi_fbr` failed miserably. Why?
        `L1 L pzp n1 0.005`
        `S1 S n1 pzn ctrl=G1`
        `G1 SYNC ton=3.51e-05s phase=0 edges=both`
        `D1 D pzp out DSCH`
        `D2 D pzn out DSCH`
        `D3 D 0 pzp DSCH`
        `D4 D 0 pzn DSCH`
        This *is* the SSHI+FBR topology. Why did it perform so poorly (vavg ~ 0.9V)?
        Maybe the `ton` was wrong? Or the $L$ value? Or the $C_1$ value?
        $C_p = 25\text{ nF}$, $L = 5\text{ mH}$.
        $t_{on} = \pi \sqrt{L C_p} = 3.14159 \times \sqrt{5\text{e-3} \times 25\text{e-9}} = 3.14159 \times \sqrt{125\text{e-12}} = 3.14159 \times 1.118\text{e-5} = 35.1\text{ }\mu\text{s}$.
        The `ton` in `sshi_fbr` was $35.1\text{ }\mu\text{s}$. The value is correct.
        But the result was $vavg = 0.93\text{ V}$. This is very low.
        The problem might be the FBR. In a standard SSHI, the inductor is used to flip the voltage, but you usually use a *half-wave* rectifier or a *synchronous* rectifier to avoid the two-diode drop of a full bridge. Or, more importantly, the inductor should be switched *after* the piezo has reached its peak.

    *   Let's try **Topology 1: SSHI with a single diode (Half-Wave)**.
        This reduces the diode drop from $2 V_f$ to $1 V_f$.
        L1: pzp to n1
        S1: n1 to pzn (Ctrl G1: both edges)
        D1: pzp to out
        C1: out to 0
        D2: out to 0 (Zener DZ33 for clamping)

    *   Let's try **Topology 2: SECE (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction)**.
        SECE usually involves an inductor and a switch that connects the piezo to the storage capacitor at the peak.
        Circuit:
        L1: pzp to n1
        S1: n1 to out (Ctrl G1: both edges)
        L2: pzn to n2
        S2: n2 to out (Ctrl G2: both edges)
        C1: out to 0
        This might be too complex. Let's look at a simpler SECE.
        One switch:
        S1: pzp to out (Wait, that's just a switch).
        Standard SECE:
        Inductor $L$ is in series with the switch.
        S1: pzp to n1, L1: n1 to out.
        At the peak, S1 closes for $t_{on}$, transferring charge.
        Since we have $pzp$ and $pzn$, we can use two of these.

    *   Let's try **Topology 3: Parallel-SSHI (P-SSHI)**.
        A P-SSHI uses a capacitor and a switch to flip the voltage. But we are limited to $L$ and $S$.

    *   Let's rethink the **Half-Wave SSHI**.
        If the piezo current is $I_p \sin(\omega t)$, the voltage is $V_p \cos(\omega t)$.
        The peaks are at $t = 0, \pi/\omega, 2\pi/\omega \dots$
        The zero crossings of the current are at $t = 0, \pi/\omega, 2\pi/\omega \dots$
        The `SYNC` controller closes the switch at the *current zero crossings* (which are the *voltage extrema*).
        If we use `edges: both`, the switch closes at $V_{max}$ and $V_{min}$.
        The inductor flips the voltage: $V_{max} \to -V_{max}$ and $V_{min} \to -V_{min}$.
        This keeps the piezo voltage oscillating.
        A diode from `pzp` to `out` will harvest the positive peaks.

    *   Let's refine the Half-Wave SSHI components:
        - L1: pzp to n1
        - S1: n1 to pzn (ctrl: G1, edges: both)
        - D1: pzp to out (DSCH)
        - C1: out to 0
        - D2: 0 to out (DZ33 for clamping)
        Wait, if I use a half-wave, I only get half the energy. Is that enough?
        $P_{load} = V^2 / R_L$.
        S2: $1.8^2 / 150\text{k} = 21.6\text{ }\mu\text{W}$.
        S4: $1.8^2 / 1\text{M} = 3.24\text{ }\mu\text{W}$.
        The piezo delivers $P_{avg} \approx \frac{1}{2} I_p V_{oc} \approx 0.5 \times 50\text{e-6} \times 3.2 \approx 80\text{ }\mu\text{W}$ (very rough).
        A half-wave should be enough.

    *   *Wait!* There is a better way to do a full-wave with SSHI:
        Use the inductor to flip the voltage, and use *two* diodes.
        D1: pzp to out
        D2: pzn to out
        Wait, if we have both D1 and D2, and we flip the voltage $V_{pzp}-V_{pzn}$, then:
        When $V_{pzp}$ is high, D1 conducts.
        When $V_{pzn}$ is high, D2 conducts.
        But $V_{pzp}$ and $V_{pzn}$ are usually opposite.
        Wait, if $V_{pzp} = V$ and $V_{pzn} = -V$, and we flip it to $V_{pzp} = -V$ and $V_{pzn} = V$.
        In both cases, one of the diodes (D1 or D2) will be forward-biased *if* $V$ is high enough.
        But we still need a return path to ground. That's why the FBR has 4 diodes.
        If we use only D1 (pzp to out) and D2 (pzn to out), we need a path from 0 back to the piezo.
        But the piezo is floating (except for the leakage resistor).
        So we *do* need the other two diodes of the bridge.

    *   Why did `sshi_fbr` fail?
        Maybe the `C1` (storage cap) was too small? $2.2\text{ }\mu\text{F}$ in the reference was okay for vavg, but here $2.2\text{e-05}$ was used. That's $22\text{ }\mu\text{F}$.
        Wait, $2.2\text{e-05}$ is $22\text{ }\mu\text{F}$, which is larger than $2.2\text{ }\mu\text{F}$.
        Let's look at the `sshi_fbr` results again. `vavg` was $0.93\text{ V}$ for S1.
        This is very low. $V_{oc}$ is 3.2V. Even a simple FBR got $2.24\text{ V}$.
        Why did adding the SSHI inductor *decrease* the voltage?
        Because the inductor/switch path is in parallel with the piezo. If the switch is closed too long or at the wrong time, it could be shorting the piezo or dissipating energy.
        But $t_{on} = 35\text{ }\mu\text{s}$ is very short.
        Wait! I see the problem. The `S1` switch in `sshi_fbr` is `n1 to pzn`.
        The inductor `L1` is `pzp to n1`.
        So the path is `pzp -> L1 -> n1 -> S1 -> pzn`.
        This is a parallel path across the piezo. This is the correct SSHI structure.
        Why did it fail?
        Maybe the `ton` was not optimal for the tuned $L$ and $C_p$?
        Or maybe the rectifier diodes were too lossy.

    *   Let's try a different approach: **Synchronous Rectification (Simplified)**.
        Since we have 2 SYNC controllers and 4 switches.
        G1 (pos peak): S1 (pzp to out), S2 (0 to pzn)
        G2 (neg peak): S3 (pzn to out), S4 (0 to pzp)
        Wait, this would be a perfect synchronous rectifier!
        Let's check:
        - At positive peak ($V_{pzp}$ max, $V_{pzn}$ min):
          S1 closes (pzp $\to$ out), S2 closes (0 $\to$ pzn).
          Current flows from piezo $\to$ pzp $\to$ out $\to$ RL $\to$ 0 $\to$ pzn $\to$ piezo.
        - At negative peak ($V_{pzp}$ min, $V_{pzn}$ max):
          S3 closes (pzn $\to$ out), S4 closes (0 $\to$ pzp).
          Current flows from piezo $\to$ pzn $\to$ out $\to$ RL $\to$ 0 $\to$ pzp $\to$ piezo.
        This is a synchronous full-bridge rectifier. No diode drops!
        This should be extremely efficient.
